issues.evidence: Kenny typed in 7-4-1-9 without thinking, and the hatch hissed open.
issues.problem: Kenny successfully enters a locked bunker by knowing the exact keypad code, but the narration gives no prior basis for him knowing it. Because this code is the only reason he can access the bunker and the radio, the plot turns on unexplained knowledge.
issues.repair: Before the hatch opens, add the smallest cause: establish that Kenny recognizes the place/code somehow, finds the code nearby, or has a memory flash tied to 7-4-1-9.

issues.evidence: Kenny woke up and there was nobody left in the world. ... Somebody was already talking.
issues.problem: The narration states as fact that nobody is left in the world, then ends with somebody apparently talking on the radio. If the voice is live, it contradicts the stated premise; if it is a recording or non-human signal, the narration does not clarify that.
issues.repair: Change the opening to Kenny’s perception, e.g. “Kenny woke up and it seemed there was nobody left in the world,” or change the ending to specify the voice is recorded/automated if no person remains.

intendedUnknowns: The impossible premise that Kenny wakes up and everyone in the world is gone.
The identity/source of the voice on the radio is presented as a final mystery or hook.

issues.evidence: "Then she remembered the screwdriver in her apron pocket, took the door's inside panel off in under a minute, and pulled the latch free."
issues.problem: The escape depends entirely on a screwdriver that is introduced only at the moment it is needed. Since the narration previously emphasizes her failed options and worsening danger, the sudden tool feels like an unearned solution rather than a consequence of established information.
issues.repair: Seed the screwdriver earlier, before she gets trapped—for example, mention that she had been tightening shelf brackets or checking repairs with a screwdriver in her apron while counting stock.

intendedUnknowns: The premise that Marta is trapped in the walk-in freezer after the door shuts behind her is accepted by design.

issues.evidence: "Jonah set off up the ridge trail at four in the afternoon, sure he'd be back at the car by six." / "It was a quarter past six when he reached the car, exactly when he'd planned."
issues.problem: The narration says Jonah planned to be back by six, but the ending says arriving at 6:15 was exactly when he planned. It also appears to be the next morning after sunrise, not the same evening, so it is not the planned time in any ordinary sense.
issues.repair: Change the final line to make the irony explicit rather than contradictory, e.g. "It was a quarter past six when he reached the car—twelve hours and fifteen minutes later than he'd planned."

intendedUnknowns: How Jonah got lost on a short trail is the premise and can remain unexplained.
The exact geography of the trail, road, and car is not specified but does not need to be.

issues.evidence: "her phone was on the kitchen counter" / "So she grabbed her phone off the counter, called her brother"
issues.problem: Priya is trapped on the roof with the ladder down, and the narration establishes the phone is inside on the kitchen counter. Nothing explains how she can reach it from the roof, so the rescue depends on an impossible action.
issues.repair: Before the call, add a plausible way she can access the phone, such as an open kitchen skylight/window within reach, or change the setup so the phone is already in her pocket.

intendedUnknowns: The premise that Priya becomes trapped on her roof when the ladder falls is accepted as given.

issues.evidence: "Cars wouldn't start. Phones were dead bricks. Even battery torches stayed dark, as if electricity itself had stopped." / "That night Ben plugged his phone into her wall socket, called his sister, and told her they were safe."
issues.problem: The narration establishes that electricity itself has stopped: phones are dead, batteries do not work, and there is no power. Without any stated change, Ben can suddenly charge/use a phone, the wall socket works, and his sister can receive a call. This breaks the core rule the viewer has just been given.
issues.repair: Before the phone call, add a clear cause that power has returned or briefly flickered back in that area; otherwise replace the call with a non-electrical way of contacting his sister.

intendedUnknowns: Why electricity has stopped working worldwide is unexplained by design under the premise.
The exact mechanism that makes even battery-powered devices fail is part of the impossible premise.

issues.evidence: “Then, for no reason he could explain, he stripped to his shorts and swam across the freezing lake in the dark, climbed out on the far side, and knocked on the door.”
issues.problem: Luis makes an extreme, dangerous choice immediately after taking the safer, rational step of calling the police. The narration explicitly says there is no reason, but gives no external trigger or established compulsion to explain why he suddenly risks hypothermia and drowning instead of waiting until morning.
issues.repair: Before he swims, add a concrete trigger or pressure: he sees someone in distress, hears a scream, notices the light signaling, sees the police will be too late, or establishes that something is compelling him toward the house.

intendedUnknowns: Why there is a light in the abandoned house across the lake is the core mystery of the premise and is allowed to remain unexplained in this excerpt.

issues.evidence: "Ada's grandmother pressed a sealed envelope into her hand and said, very seriously, do not open this until midnight, whatever happens." / "Ada walked home happy and went to bed early."
issues.problem: The narration opens with the envelope and the midnight rule as the central promise, but the story never returns to the envelope, midnight, or whether Ada opens it. Since this is all the viewer will hear, the main setup is dropped rather than paid off, investigated, or deliberately carried forward.
issues.repair: Before the ending, reconnect the school-day conflict to the envelope or explicitly carry it forward: e.g. have Ada notice the envelope before bed and choose not to open it until midnight, or end with midnight arriving and her reaching for it.

intendedUnknowns: What is inside the envelope and why it must wait until midnight are unexplained by design in the premise.

issues.evidence: "Then a coastguard helicopter appeared out of the cloud, though nobody knew he was out there, and lowered a man on a line."
issues.problem: The rescue is the story’s resolution, but the narration explicitly says nobody knew Rory was out there. With the radio gone and no other distress signal or search reason established, the helicopter’s arrival has no causal basis and feels like rescue by coincidence.
issues.repair: Seed an earlier reason the coastguard can find him: for example, Rory had filed a float plan, activated an EPIRB, fired a flare, or the helicopter was already searching the area for another vessel.

intendedUnknowns: The engine dying in a storm ten miles offshore is the premise and does not need further explanation.
The storm’s sudden arrival and the exact mechanical details of the engine failure can remain unexplained.

issues.evidence: "Kenny woke up to forty-seven missed calls. Every single one was from his own phone number."
issues.problem: The narration opens with a strong mystery, especially that the calls came from Kenny's own number, but the rest of the piece never investigates it, explains it, or clearly frames it as a mystery being deliberately carried forward. The viewer is left with the apparent central premise dropped.
issues.repair: Add an early beat where Kenny engages with the calls—tries calling back, checks voicemail, contacts the phone company, notices a message, or consciously decides to ignore it for a stated reason—and either pay it off later or clearly leave it as an intentional unresolved mystery.

intendedUnknowns: Kenny waking up to dozens of missed calls is the allowed premise.

issues.evidence: “the radio said the pass would be closed for two days and temperatures would fall to minus twenty. She had a quarter tank of fuel and no blanket.” / “She sat in the driver's seat and ate a slice, wondering who was getting married, and decided she'd write them a card.”
issues.problem: The narration establishes a life-threatening survival problem, then ends on the cake/card beat without engaging whether her fuel, heat, or rescue problem has changed. A viewer may feel the main danger has been quietly set aside rather than left as a deliberate unresolved ending.
issues.repair: Before or during the cake beat, add a small line showing the survival stakes remain active or are being managed, e.g. that she times another engine burst, rations the cake, or writes the card while waiting out the first night.

intendedUnknowns: Whether Tasha ultimately survives the two days stranded in the blizzard is not answered in the narration.
Who was getting married is explicitly framed as something Tasha wonders about, not information the viewer is expected to have.
Why Tuesday is repeating for Nell is the central impossible premise and is allowed.
Who the old man is, how he knows the count, and what he means by “the last one” are presented as a closing mystery/hook rather than explained in this excerpt.

issues.evidence: “Kenny didn't turn the broadcast off that night.”
issues.problem: The story bible requires second-person, present-tense narration, but this narration is third-person and past tense throughout. It contradicts the established narrative perspective the viewer is meant to hear.
issues.repair: Change the narration into second person and present tense from the first line, e.g. “You don’t turn the broadcast off that night.”

intendedUnknowns: Who wrote the notes is deliberately unexplained at this point.
Who or what “they” are is deliberately unexplained at this point.
How the note-writer got into the radio booth and cut the cable can remain a suspense mystery for later.

issues.location: “He'd never been inside the radio station...”
issues.evidence: “He'd never been inside the radio station, he realised, never even noticed it was there.”
issues.problem: This directly contradicts the established Part 1 continuity that Kenny broadcast from the radio station above the bakery. If he used that station to broadcast his name, street, and meeting point, he cannot now realize he has never been inside it or never noticed it existed.
issues.repair: Change the line so Kenny has been inside the station before, but notices something new about it now — for example, that he had never explored the back rooms, the transmitter cabinet, or a second locked studio.

issues.evidence: “His dog Biscuit trotted beside him, nose down, the only other living thing he'd seen all week.”
issues.problem: The story bible says Kenny lives alone and has seen no living creature since everyone vanished. Giving him a dog who has been with him all week contradicts both constraints, and also changes the premise that he is alone.
issues.repair: Remove Biscuit, or establish Biscuit as a new discovery in the moment rather than a companion he has had all week — but that would still need to engage with the major twist that Kenny has finally found a living creature.

issues.location: “and then walked to the bakery on Fifth”
issues.evidence: “Kenny switched the broadcast off the moment he read the note, and then walked to the bakery on Fifth to think.”
issues.problem: Part 1 established that Kenny broadcast from the radio station above the bakery. This narration implies he was somewhere else when he switched the broadcast off, then walked to the bakery afterward. Unless he has a remote shutoff, the broadcast equipment should be at the bakery/radio station location.
issues.repair: Clarify that he reads the note at the station/bakery, or have him walk to the radio station first and switch the broadcast off there.

issues.evidence: “At the bakery the bread on the racks was still warm. Somebody had baked it that morning.”
issues.problem: The established premise is that Kenny has seen no living creature since everyone vanished. Stating as fact that somebody baked the bread that morning implies another person is present and active, which contradicts the empty-world setup unless the story frames this as a shocking mystery or Kenny’s inference rather than confirmed fact.
issues.repair: Make it an inference or mystery: for example, “It was as if somebody had baked it that morning,” or have Kenny react to the impossibility of fresh bread in an empty bakery.

intendedUnknowns: Why Kenny is alone in an empty world is part of the premise.
Who wrote the note, and who or what “they” refers to, is part of the initiating premise and not an audit issue by itself.

issues.evidence: "She called her sister and it died mid-ring." / "Then he said the police had been on the phone all night. A woman had called them, frantic, because her sister's call had cut off mid-ring on the last bus home."
issues.problem: The police response is said to have lasted "all night" and included searching every stop, but the stated trigger was Dana's call cutting off mid-ring, which happened only after she woke up in the depot and shortly before she reached the office. There is not enough time for the sister to call police, the police to contact the depot, the driver to deny seeing her, and a route-wide search to have already been happening all night.
issues.repair: Establish earlier that Dana was already missing for hours before the mid-ring call, or change the ending so the sister and police have only just started calling around rather than having searched all night.

intendedUnknowns: Dana being accidentally locked inside the bus is the central premise; the narration acknowledges the driver claimed the bus was empty, and Dana was hidden under her coat on the back seat.
Why Mara's car has been moving at night is presented as the central mystery and is answered by the reveal that her father and son are using it for secret driving practice.
Her father's involvement is initially misleading because his eyesight and country music point toward him as the driver, but the later reveal deliberately overturns that assumption.
Why everyone has vanished from Kenny's world.
How the new world keeps human-built systems running without people.
Who wrote the note under Kenny's door.
Who or what “They” are in “They can hear it too.”
Whether Kenny is truly alone or whether the note reveals another presence.
What Marcus’s brother means by “it” in “She's going to be weird about it” is left as a final twist/mystery rather than explained in this narration.
The coincidence that both Priya and Marcus are being told to “act normal” is the comic premise/twist.
Why the voice can address Jess by name despite seeming to come through an old monitor channel.
Who the woman on the monitor is, and whether she is the neighbor, an intruder, or something supernatural.
Why the voice tells Jess to close her daughter’s window.
